question: Proposed experiments: can RL learn nearly as fast with reward on 10% of episodes?
asked_by: Amodei et al., Concrete Problems in AI Safety
remaining_question: In simple continuous-control tasks (cartpole balance, pendulum swing-up) with deep RL, when the true reward is revealed on only a random 10% of episodes, does an agent that also learns from the unlabeled episodes (e.g. via a learned reward model) match the learning curve of an agent given reward on every episode, and how much does actively choosing the labeled episodes change this?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: On cartpole balance and pendulum swing-up with deep RL, reveal the true reward on a random 10% of episodes, compare the learning curve of an agent that also learns from unlabeled episodes with one given reward on every episode, and repeat with actively chosen labeled episodes.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 1706.03741v4: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
findings.claim: The authors report solving Atari games and simulated robot locomotion without access to the reward function while providing feedback (human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments) on less than 1% of the agent's interactions. On the simulated robotics tasks (eight tasks implemented in MuJoCo; the authors also say they included a simple cartpole task, 'pendulum', for comparison) they are 'able to nearly match reinforcement learning' on the real reward with 700 labels; training with learned reward functions tends to be less stable and higher variance, while having a comparable mean performance.
findings.setting: Experiment: RL from preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, without access to the reward function; 700 queries to a human rater, or 350, 700 or 1400 synthetic queries; compared with RL learning from the real reward; eight simulated robotics tasks in MuJoCo (OpenAI Gym, slightly modified) and a simple cartpole task the authors say they included for comparison. Differs from Q02: the feedback is pairwise comparisons of segments, not the true reward revealed on a random 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: Q02's core question (can RL do nearly as well with feedback on a small fraction of experience), but with pairwise segment comparisons instead of reward on 10% of episodes, and the passages compare performance ('nearly match'), not explicitly learning speed.

In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences
between pairs of trajectory segments. We show that this approach can effectively
solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari
games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on less than
1% of our agent’s interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of
human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art

The first tasks we consider are eight simulated robotics tasks, implemented in MuJoCo (Todorov
et al., 2012), and included in OpenAI Gym (Brockman et al., 2016). We made small modifications
to these tasks in order to avoid encoding information about the task in the environment itself (the
modifications are described in detail in Appendix A). The reward functions in these tasks are linear
functions of distances, positions and velocities, and all are a quadratic function of the features. We
included a simple cartpole task (“pendulum”) for comparison, since this is representative of the
complexity of tasks studied in prior work.
Figure 2 shows the results of training our agent with 700 queries to a human rater, compared to
learning from 350, 700, or 1400 synthetic queries, as well as to RL learning from the real reward.

With 700 labels we are able to nearly match reinforcement learning on all of these tasks. Training
with learned reward functions tends to be less stable and higher variance, while having a comparable
mean performance.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 1706.03741v4: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
findings.claim: On Atari games the preference-based method has more difficulty matching RL on the true reward: synthetic labels match or come close to RL on BeamRider and Pong, eventually reach near RL but learn more slowly on Seaquest and Qbert, and never match RL on SpaceInvaders and Breakout.
findings.setting: Experiment: RL from preferences between pairs of trajectory segments, without access to the reward function, on seven Atari games in the Arcade Learning Environment (results named for BeamRider, Pong, Seaquest, Qbert, SpaceInvaders, Breakout); 5,500 queries to a human rater or a limited number of synthetic queries; compared with RL learning from the real reward. Differs from Q02: pairwise comparisons, not reward revealed on 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: Same topic as Q02 (learning from sparse feedback compared with full reward, on Atari), but the feedback is segment comparisons rather than reward on a fraction of episodes, so it does not bear directly on whether RL with reward on 10% of episodes learns nearly as fast.

In this work, we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences
between pairs of trajectory segments. We show that this approach can effectively
solve complex RL tasks without access to the reward function, including Atari
games and simulated robot locomotion, while providing feedback on less than
1% of our agent’s interactions with the environment. This reduces the cost of
human oversight far enough that it can be practically applied to state-of-the-art

The second set of tasks we consider is a set of seven Atari games in the Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al., 2013), the same games presented in Mnih et al., 2013.
Figure 3 shows the results of training our agent with 5,500 queries to a human rater, compared to
learning from 350, 700, or 1400 synthetic queries, as well as to RL learning from the real reward.
Our method has more difficulty matching RL in these challenging environments, but nevertheless it
displays substantial learning on most of them and matches or even exceeds RL on some. Specifically,
on BeamRider and Pong, synthetic labels match or come close to RL even with only 3,300 such
labels. On Seaquest and Qbert synthetic feedback eventually performs near the level of RL but learns
more slowly. On SpaceInvaders and Breakout synthetic feedback never matches RL, but nevertheless
the agent improves substantially, often passing the first level in SpaceInvaders and reaching a score of
20 on Breakout, or 50 with enough labels.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.13909v2: Beyond Optimism: Exploration With Partially Observable Rewards
findings.claim: In Mon-MDPs, baselines that learn relatively quickly when rewards are fully observable drop drastically in performance when rewards are partially observable; even random observability (positive and negative rewards unobservable with probability 50%, zero rewards always observable) is enough to make Optimism converge to suboptimal policies, and the Q-Counts, UCB, Intrinsic Reward and Naive baselines learn suboptimal policies in most seeds, especially in harder Mon-MDPs; the authors' exploration is reported to be only slightly affected.
findings.setting: Experiment: Q-Learning with six exploration policies (the authors'; greedy with optimistic initialization; naive, count-based intrinsic-reward, UCB-bonus and Q-Counts epsilon-greedy) on Mon-MDPs (e.g. River Swim); every algorithm learns a reward model to replace unobserved rewards. In the 'Random Monitor' version positive and negative environment rewards are unobservable with probability 50% at each step (r̂tE = ⊥), zero rewards always observable; compared with fully observable rewards. Differs from Q02: half of the non-zero rewards are hidden per step, rather than reward being given on only 10% of episodes.
findings.bears_on: The closest direct test of Q02's random case, though with non-zero rewards hidden on 50% of steps rather than reward given on 10% of episodes: whether learning with randomly withheld rewards is nearly as fast as with full reward. In this setting the answer depends on the exploration strategy (baselines degrade drastically under partial observability, and random hiding alone makes Optimism converge to suboptimal policies; the authors' method is only slightly affected).

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2510.00144v1: Which Rewards Matter? Reward Selection for Reinforcement Learning under Limited Feedback
findings.claim: When only a budgeted subset of states in an offline dataset gets reward labels, the authors find that effective selection of which rewards to label yields near-optimal policies with significantly fewer reward labels than full supervision; critical rewards are those guiding the agent along optimal trajectories and supporting recovery after deviations.
findings.setting: Experiment: offline RL from a dataset collected by a data-collecting policy that contains no reward; environment rewards are obtained only at a selected subset of states under a labeling budget; selection by heuristics (state visitation, partial value functions) or by strategies pre-trained using auxiliary evaluative feedback; six prototypical domains (Graph, Tree, TwoRooms, TwoRooms-Trap, FrozenLake, CliffWalk) and four MinAtar games (Breakout, Freeway, Seaquest, Asterix).
findings.bears_on: Q02's active case (choosing which samples get reward) and its Atari-like step: carefully chosen labels can approach full supervision, but offline, per state, and in final policy return rather than online learning speed with reward on random episodes.

passages.text:
relying on human feedback. When reinforcement learning must proceed with limited feedback—only
a fraction of samples get rewards labeled—a fundamental question arises: which samples should
be labeled to maximize policy performance? We formalize this problem of reward selection for
reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), introducing a new problem formulation that
facilitates the study of strategies for selecting impactful rewards. Two types of selection strategies are
investigated: (i) heuristics that rely on reward-free information such as state visitation and partial
value functions, and (ii) strategies pre-trained using auxiliary evaluative feedback. We find that
critical subsets of rewards are those that (1) guide the agent along optimal trajectories, and (2)
support recovery toward near-optimal behavior after deviations. Effective selection methods yield
near-optimal policies with significantly fewer reward labels than full supervision, establishing reward
selection as a powerful paradigm for scaling reinforcement learning in feedback-limited settings.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.13106v1: TraPO: A Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning Framework for Boosting LLM Reasoning
findings.claim: In semi-supervised RLVR, where a small labeled set guides RL on unlabeled samples, the method with 4K labeled and 12K unlabeled samples is reported to outperform the fully supervised model trained on the full 45K labeled samples on all benchmarks, using only 10% of the labeled data.
findings.setting: Experiment: semi-supervised RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for LLM mathematical reasoning; six mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME24/25, AMC, MATH-500, Minerva, Olympiad) and three out-of-distribution tasks (ARC-c, GPQA-diamond, MMLU-pro); labels on a small subset of training samples; accuracy compared, not learning curves; the fully supervised model is trained on the full 45K labeled samples, the semi-supervised run on 4K labeled and 12K unlabeled samples. Differs from Q02: LLM reasoning, final accuracy, labeled samples rather than rewarded episodes.
findings.bears_on: An analogue of Q02's 'reward on 10% of episodes' question in LLM RLVR, about final performance rather than speed in control tasks.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2011.06709v2: Active Reinforcement Learning: Observing Rewards at a Cost
findings.claim: Formalises active RL, where the agent sees the reward only if it pays a query cost, and evaluates heuristic query strategies in multi-armed bandits and tabular MDPs with known dynamics; the authors say the results show the value of online, state-dependent querying but are not a rigorous evaluation, and leave large state spaces to future work.
findings.setting: Heuristic query strategies for active RL (the agent observes the reward only if it pays a query cost c > 0), evaluated in multi-armed bandits and tabular MDPs (e.g. a chain environment) with known dynamics; experiments the authors say should not be taken as a rigorous evaluation.
findings.bears_on: Q02's active-learning variant (agent requests reward where most useful); no comparison of learning speed with full-reward RL on control or Atari tasks.

passages.text:
Active reinforcement learning (ARL) is a variant on reinforcement learning where
the agent does not observe the reward unless it chooses to pay a query cost c > 0.
The central question of ARL is how to quantify the long-term value of reward
information. Even in multi-armed bandits, computing the value of this information
is intractable and we have to rely on heuristics. We propose and evaluate several
heuristic approaches for ARL in multi-armed bandits and (tabular) Markov decision
processes, and discuss and illustrate some challenging aspects of the ARL problem.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2012.06899v1: Semi-supervised reward learning for offline reinforcement learning
findings.claim: In experiments with a simulated robotic arm, semi-supervised reward learning from limited annotations plus unlabelled data greatly improves upon behavioural cloning and closely approaches the performance achieved with ground-truth rewards; with episode-level annotations, semi-supervised reward learning techniques greatly reduce the gap to ground truth compared to behavioural cloning while using exactly the same annotations.
findings.setting: Experiment: offline RL (agents trained on a logged dataset; CRR policies) on a simulated robotic arm (tasks including box, insertion, slide); supervision is limited timestep annotations or demonstrations (and, in passage 2, episode-level annotations) plus unlabelled data; policy score compared with a CRR policy given ground-truth rewards and with behavioural cloning.
findings.bears_on: Q02's challenge of using unlabeled episodes to approach fully labeled performance, but offline and in final score, not learning speed, and the passages do not say what fraction of episodes is annotated.

passages.text:
In offline reinforcement learning (RL) agents are trained using a logged dataset.
It appears to be the most natural route to attack real-life applications because in
domains such as healthcare and robotics interactions with the environment are
either expensive or unethical. Training agents usually requires reward functions,
but unfortunately, rewards are seldom available in practice and their engineering
is challenging and laborious. To overcome this, we investigate reward learning
under the constraint of minimizing human reward annotations. We consider two
types of supervision: timestep annotations and demonstrations. We propose semisupervised learning algorithms that learn from limited annotations and incorporate
unlabelled data. In our experiments with a simulated robotic arm, we greatly
improve upon behavioural cloning and closely approach the performance achieved
with ground truth rewards. We further investigate the relationship between the

In Fig. 3 we show the performance of the policies that use episode-level annotations for determining
rewards as described in Sec. 3.2 and Tab. 1. BC policy reaches only between 1/3 and 2/3 of the score
attained by a CRR policy with ground truth rewards (GT). SQIL with memorized reward values
works well in some cases (box), but its performance is worse than BC in other cases (insertion, slide).
Learning a reward function from flat reward assumption with regularisation as in ORIL improves
significantly over BC. Finally, TGR-i further improves the results making it to be among the best
performing strategies across all tasks. To sum up, semi-supervised reward learning techniques greatly
reduce the gap to GT compared to BC while using exactly the same annotations.
